title: Visualising a line

D0.outcome: Explains why calculation means tracking the pieces and attacked squares, not a mental picture of the board.

D1.outcome: For a named candidate, states the position after the next two plies and which piece is then attacked, with the board visible but no pieces moved.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether a three-ply line loses a piece (including an uncovered attack) without moving pieces, in at least 7 of 10.

D3.outcome: Holds a five-ply forcing line with a capture and a check, then lists the legal replies and the attacked pieces at the end of it.

D4.outcome: In own games, writes down the position after the intended line and the expected reply for chosen moves, and the record matches the game in at least 8 of 10.

misconceptions: Visualising is seeing a clear picture; it is better built by tracking what moved and what is now attacked.
A longer line is better; accuracy past the first capture matters more than length.
sources: docs/curriculum-map-v1.md §2 S4 (Kotov, Aagaard, Ramesh, Dvoretsky, Rowson, Heisman, all [R] in the map)
sources/sheets/capablanca_chess-fundamentals.md §4 CI-17 (d) (calculation by visualising future positions is what counts)
conditions: Lines are short and the learner re-anchors on attacked pieces after each move.
Captures and discovered attacks are the points where tracking fails.
contrasts: Forgetting which piece a capture removed, so the final position is wrong.
A knight route miscounted by one move (opposite corners need six).
A one-move tactic that needs no line tracking.

soft_prereq_notes.FND.PIECE.KNIGHT.D1: knight routes are the hardest to track
